# Albright & Marsh Group — Pricing Diagnostic Pack

Confidential management pack prepared for the partner-led pricing
strategy review. Fully synthetic — written for fixture use only —
shaped like a real boutique-firm engagement input.

## Company snapshot

Albright & Marsh Group is a UK-headquartered multi-segment retailer
trading FY24 revenue of £203m at a blended gross margin of 36.4%
and group EBITDA of £21.7m (10.7% margin). The business operates
four reporting segments: Food (own-brand grocery), Premium
(specialty foods), Home (homewares and small appliances), and
Online (D2C marketplace). The estate is 142 stores plus the online
channel; FY24 like-for-like (LFL) sales growth was +2.1% blended
but ranged from -3.4% (Home) to +6.8% (Online).

The company is sponsor-owned (Marylebone Equity, vintage 2020)
with a stated 24-month exit window. The pricing review is the
sponsor's third value-creation initiative; the prior two
(supply-chain consolidation and store-network rationalisation)
delivered £4.1m and £6.3m run-rate EBITDA respectively against
plan.

## Segment-level financials (FY24)

| Segment  | Revenue (£m) | Gross margin | EBITDA (£m) | LFL growth | Stores |
|----------|--------------|--------------|-------------|------------|--------|
| Food     | 102.4        | 22.1%        | 8.1         | +1.4%      | 84     |
| Premium  | 38.7         | 47.3%        | 6.9         | +2.8%      | 32     |
| Home     | 37.6         | 39.8%        | 3.2         | -3.4%      | 26     |
| Online   | 24.3         | 33.2%        | 3.5         | +6.8%      | n/a    |
| **Group**| **203.0**    | **36.4%**    | **21.7**    | **+2.1%**  | **142**|

Food carries the lowest gross margin but the highest revenue base
and the most pricing volume to defend. Premium is the highest-
margin segment; Home is the only segment in absolute decline; Online
is the highest-growth segment and the only one with structurally
expanding contribution margin.

Customer cohort retention by segment (12-month repeat purchase rate
for the FY23 acquisition cohort, observed through end-FY24):

- Food:    62.4%
- Premium: 71.8%
- Home:    44.2%
- Online:  58.7%

Premium retention is healthy; Food retention is at the sector
median; Home retention is the structural concern (well below the
sector 60% benchmark for non-grocery formats).

## Competitor pricing positioning (FY24 H2 audit)

Audit conducted on a sample basket of 412 SKUs across the four
segments, benchmarked against the four most relevant comparators
in each. Index = 100 means parity with the comparator basket on
matched items.

| Segment  | Comparator set                              | Index vs comp | Headroom |
|----------|---------------------------------------------|---------------|----------|
| Food     | Aldi, Lidl, Sainsbury's basics, Asda        | 108.4         | 4-6% down|
| Premium  | Waitrose, Whole Foods Market, Selfridges    | 96.2          | 3-5% up  |
| Home     | The Range, B&M, Dunelm                      | 112.7         | 8-10% down|
| Online   | Amazon, Argos online, John Lewis online     | 102.1         | n/a      |

Food prices index ~8% above the discounter pair and ~4% above the
mid-tier grocers. Premium prices index 4 points BELOW the premium
comparator basket — a pricing headroom case the prior partner
flagged but never tested. Home prices index 13% above the
out-of-town value players, the principal explanatory factor for
the negative LFL.

## Customer willingness-to-pay (Q4 FY24 study)

The firm commissioned a stated-preference study run on 1,800
respondents across the four customer segments. Top findings:

- **Premium customers** show price elasticity of -0.8 on the
  category basket — willingness to absorb a 5-7% price uplift
  on differentiated SKUs without measurable defection. Anchor
  insight: Premium customers cite "consistency of stocking" and
  "in-store experience" above price as decision drivers in 64%
  of category responses.
- **Food shoppers** show elasticity of -1.6 on staples and -0.9
  on private label — staple-pricing increases trigger immediate
  basket-mix shifts to discounters; private-label increases are
  better absorbed.
- **Home customers** show elasticity of -2.1 on big-ticket items
  (>£40 ASP) and -1.4 on the long tail. The high big-ticket
  elasticity confirms the LFL data: Home is structurally
  price-sensitive at the SKU level Albright competes on.
- **Online customers** show the lowest blended elasticity (-0.6)
  but the highest trial-rate response (+18% trial uplift on
  promotional pricing) — the channel's pricing power is
  promotional rather than structural.

## Cost structure decomposition

FY24 P&L decomposed by segment with FY22 baseline for the
two-year walk:

- Group COGS rate moved from 61.8% (FY22) to 63.6% (FY24), a
  180bps deterioration driven by Food (220bps) and Home
  (280bps). Premium and Online held rate within ±30bps.
- Group opex rate held at 25.7% (FY22) → 25.8% (FY24); the
  apparent stability masks a 90bps rise in marketing offset by
  a 120bps fall in store payroll (post-rationalisation).
- Working capital cycle: 38 days (FY22) → 51 days (FY24). Food
  and Home together explain 12 of the 13 day deterioration —
  inventory builds in both, partly cyclical, partly the
  symptom of slowing turn.

## Implementation constraints

- The board has signed off on supplier-side renegotiations Q1 FY25
  but has explicitly excluded SKU rationalisation from the H1 plan
  on customer-experience concerns.
- Marketing budget is fixed at FY24 levels (£8.4m) for FY25;
  no additional pricing-test budget approved.
- The sponsor's exit window (24 months) caps the realistic payback
  horizon at 18 months — actions requiring 24m+ payback are out
  of scope.
- Albright operates a single ERP (SAP S/4HANA, deployed FY22) so
  segment-level price changes are technically feasible within a
  3-week change cycle.

## Specific actions requested by the partner

1. Identify segment-specific pricing actions with quantified £
   revenue impact at conservative, base, and aggressive sensitivity.
2. Specify the customer-segment-by-action 2x2 matrix (price action
   on one axis, willingness-to-pay confidence on the other) so
   the partner can read the recommendation in 30 seconds.
3. Produce a 90-day implementation roadmap with named owners
   (Pricing Director, CFO, Head of Category for each segment) and
   gating decisions (week-2 alignment, week-6 system change, week-
   12 LFL read).
4. Flag any actions that cannot survive the 18-month exit-window
   constraint and recommend an alternative within scope.

These are the four deliverable constraints the engagement memo
must address. They are non-negotiable for sign-off.
